explanation: Version control tracks every file change over time. Think of it as a time machine for your project — you can always go back to any saved point.
tip: The 'version' in version control refers to each saved state (snapshot) of your project.

explanation: In a distributed system, every developer has the full repository. No internet? No problem — you can still commit, branch, and review history locally.
tip: Compare: Subversion (SVN) is centralized — you need the server to do almost anything.

explanation: Git is software you install. GitHub is a website. You can use Git without GitHub, but GitHub requires Git to work.
tip: Think of Git as WhatsApp and GitHub as the server that stores your messages in the cloud.

explanation: Linus Torvalds needed a replacement for BitKeeper in 2005. He wrote the first version of Git in just a few days.
tip: Fun fact: Git was self-hosted — the first commit of Git was managed by Git itself.

explanation: Every clone is a full copy. Run `git log` on your laptop with no Wi-Fi and you will still see the entire project history.
tip: This is why `git clone` takes some time for large projects — it downloads everything.

explanation: Merge conflicts happen when two people edit the same part of a file. Git detects this and asks you to resolve it manually — safely.
tip: Before Git, teams used to lock files so only one person could edit at a time. Git made parallel work safe.

explanation: A repo is more than just files. The hidden `.git` folder inside your project contains the entire history — every commit, every branch.
tip: If you delete the `.git` folder, your project loses all its version history instantly.

explanation: GitLab is fully open-source and can be self-hosted. Bitbucket is popular in enterprise environments. GitHub is the most popular for open source.
tip: Git Bash is a terminal emulator for Windows — not a hosting platform.

explanation: Your local repository is self-contained. GitHub only stores a remote copy. The local copy is what matters for your day-to-day work.
tip: This is a key advantage of distributed VCS over centralized systems like SVN.

explanation: A commit is a snapshot with a message, timestamp, and author. It does NOT automatically push to GitHub — that requires a separate `git push` command.
tip: Think of a commit as saving a checkpoint in a game — it stays local until you decide to sync.
